entities.summary:
Alternative for Germany (AfD) is a far-right political party founded on February 6, 2013, in Berlin, emerging from the backdrop of the European financial crisis and the subsequent influx of refugees. The party gained traction as a response to perceived failures of mainstream parties in addressing immigration, national identity, and European Union policies, positioning itself as a defender of traditional German values. Key figures in the party's rise include Bernd Lucke, one of the initial leaders, and Frauke Petry, who later became a prominent spokesperson.

The party's initial success was marked by its participation in the 2014 European Parliament elections, where it secured 7.1% of the vote, enabling it to send its first representatives to Brussels. As it capitalized on growing anti-immigrant sentiment, particularly during the refugee crisis of 2015, the AfD's rhetoric became increasingly nationalist and anti-Islam. By the 2017 federal elections, the party had garnered 12.6% of the vote, making it the third-largest party in the Bundestag, a significant milestone for a far-right party in post-war Germany.

The legacy of the AfD has been contentious, reshaping the political landscape in Germany and influencing debates on immigration and integration across Europe. Its emergence has galvanized other right-wing movements, prompting a reevaluation of political discourse surrounding nationalism and identity in a globalized world. Moreover, the party's presence has led to increased polarization within German society, challenging the traditional consensus politics that have characterized the post-war era.

As historian Jan Zielonka remarked, 'The rise of the AfD reflects a profound discontent with the established political order, revealing deep societal fractures.' The party's ability to harness public sentiment has resulted in lasting changes to the political fabric of Germany and beyond, making it a crucial case study for understanding contemporary populism in Europe.
